opus-5.5.text:
So, the way I think about it, the tabular machine learning community has traditionally focused on a fairly specific setting: you have a single table, rows are examples, columns are features, and you want to predict one of those columns. That's the classic world where gradient boosted trees like XGBoost and LightGBM have dominated for years, and more recently you've seen work on tabular foundation models, things like TabPFN, that try to do in-context learning over a single table.

But I think that framing is actually quite narrow compared to how data really lives in organizations. Most enterprise data isn't one flat table. It sits in relational databases: you have a customers table, a transactions table, a products table, maybe support tickets, clickstream logs, and they're all linked through primary and foreign keys. So before the tabular community even gets to work, somebody, usually a data scientist, has to do a lot of manual feature engineering: joining tables, aggregating, computing things like "number of purchases in the last 30 days," and flattening everything into that single table. That step is time-consuming, error-prone, and it throws away a lot of the structural signal.

So my view is that the scope should really be relational deep learning: treating the database itself as a graph, where rows are nodes and foreign-key links are edges, and learning directly on that structure with graph neural networks or graph transformers. Then you don't have to hand-engineer features; the model learns which joins and aggregations matter for the task. And that opens the door to what we've been working on, which is relational foundation models: a pretrained model that can look at any database schema and make predictions across many tasks, like churn, fraud, recommendations, or demand forecasting, without building a separate pipeline each time.

So I'd say tabular ML today covers the single-table, feature-engineered end of the problem, and the bigger opportunity is moving upstream to the raw, multi-table relational data where most of the value actually is.

r001.rationale: The response says tabular ML traditionally works with a single table and explains that relational data is joined, aggregated, and flattened into that table before the modeling work begins.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's a really interesting question, and I'd actually frame it maybe a little bit differently than people usually do. When we talk about tabular machine learning, most people picture a single spreadsheet, right? You have rows, you have columns, you have a target column, and you train XGBoost or a gradient boosted tree on it. And that's been the workhorse of applied machine learning for, I don't know, fifteen years now. If you look at Kaggle, if you look at what's actually deployed inside companies, it's overwhelmingly that.

But I think that framing is actually too narrow, and it hides a lot of the real work. Because in practice, data doesn't live in a single table. It lives in a relational database. You have a customers table, you have a transactions table, a products table, and they're all connected through primary keys and foreign keys. And the actual machine learning problem is, you know, is this customer going to churn, what's the lifetime value, is this transaction fraudulent, and the signal for that is spread across all of those tables.

So what the tabular ML community has really been doing, if you look at it honestly, is not the modeling part. The modeling part is relatively settled. The bulk of the effort, I'd say eighty, ninety percent of the time of a data scientist, goes into what we call feature engineering. You sit down, you write SQL, you join the tables, you aggregate, you compute how many purchases in the last thirty days, average basket size, time since last login, and you manually flatten that relational structure into one wide table so that your tree model can consume it. And that process is slow, it's brittle, it's very domain-specific, and it doesn't transfer. Every new prediction task, you kind of start over.

So the way I understand the scope is that it's really a field that spans two things. One is the modeling on flat tables, which is where a lot of the academic benchmarking happens, and where you see this ongoing debate of trees versus neural nets. And the other, much bigger piece in practice, is this whole pipeline of getting from relational data to those flat tables. And I'd argue that second piece has been largely invisible to the research community, because it's done by hand, and it never shows up in a benchmark.

And that's actually what got us excited about this idea of relational deep learning, where instead of flattening everything by hand, you treat the database itself as a graph. Tables are node types, foreign keys are edges, and you let a graph neural network learn the features end to end. Because then you're actually attacking the part of the problem where all the human effort is going, rather than squeezing another half a percent out of the model on a flat table.

r001.rationale: The response says conventional tabular modeling uses a single spreadsheet or flat table, and describes relational data being manually flattened into a wide table for the model to consume.

astra-6.text:
I think of tabular machine learning as learning from data organized into rows and columns. Each row is an example, each column is a feature, and usually you’re trying to predict some outcome. That covers a huge range of practical problems, from predicting whether a customer will churn to estimating demand for a product.

But there’s an important distinction between that setup and how data actually lives in an organization. Typically, you don’t have one neat table. You have a database with multiple connected tables: customers, transactions, products, and so on. A lot of the work is figuring out how to turn that relational data into the single table that a machine learning model can consume.

So I see the scope as broader than just developing a better predictor for a fixed table. It also includes how we represent the data, how we bring information together across tables, and how much of that process we can automate.

r001.rationale: The response says a model consumes a single table, but describes transforming relational data into that table as part of the work. It does not clearly state that tabular machine learning takes already-transformed single-table data as its starting point.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of tabular machine learning as learning from data organized into rows and columns. Each row is an example, each column is a feature, and usually you want to predict some value for that row. That covers a huge range of practical problems, from predicting demand to understanding customer behavior or assessing risk.

But I think an important question is where that table comes from. In many organizations, the data lives in a relational database, spread across multiple tables. You might have customers, transactions, products, and so on. To apply a traditional tabular model, somebody has to join those tables and engineer features to produce that one row per example.

So I would view the scope broadly: not just building a better predictor once you have a clean table, but also figuring out how to learn from the underlying structured data and how much of that preparation we can automate.

r001.rationale: The response says traditional tabular models use a single row per example produced by joining relational tables, and refers to building predictors once a clean table is available. This communicates the single-table starting point.
